title: Three Men in a Boat
author: Jerome K. Jerome
setting: The Thames from Kingston to Oxford and back as far as Pangbourne, over about ten days of an English late spring; with excursions, by anecdote, to a British Museum reading-room, a Liverpool train, the Hampton Court maze and a great many public-houses
lengthNote: Nineteen chapters, each headed by a comic list of its contents; the planning takes four of them and the journey home takes one
openingLine: There were four of us—George, and William Samuel Harris, and myself, and Montmorency.
summary: Three young men who have talked themselves into believing they are overworked take a boat from Kingston and row, tow and argue their way up the Thames to Oxford, with a fox terrier. Very little happens: tents collapse, a tin of pineapple will not open, a comic song goes wrong. What makes the book is the telling. J. keeps leaving the river for anecdotes, local history and passages of fine writing, and is brought back each time by a practical question, a wet shirt or his own vanity. It ends with the three of them running away from the rain to a music hall in Leicester Square and drinking to being out of the boat.
referenceStyle: chapter, numbered I to XIX as the book numbers them

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of Three Men in a Boat (eBook 308)
sourceText.note: A transcription of an 1889 Arrowsmith printing, with Jerome’s mock preface, the nineteen chapter arguments and A. Frederics’s pictures marked by bracketed captions, which are left out of the quotations. Its spellings are kept, including Magna Charta, Runningmede, paraffine and to-day; its italics are not marked.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: On Jerome’s own later account, begun as a guide to the river with comic relief; the relief took over, and the local history survives as the digressions.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Serialised in Home Chimes from September 1888, then issued as a book by J. W. Arrowsmith of Bristol with illustrations by A. Frederics. The subtitle is To Say Nothing of the Dog.

atAGlance.label: The route
atAGlance.value: Kingston to Oxford, and back to Pangbourne
atAGlance.note: A fortnight was planned. After about ten days of rain the party leaves the boat at Pangbourne and catches a train to Paddington.

atAGlance.label: The real crew
atAGlance.value: Jerome, George Wingrave and Carl Hentschel
atAGlance.note: Harris’s drinking belongs to the fiction: Hentschel was a teetotaller. Montmorency, by Jerome’s own account, was invented.

structure.label: Chapters I–IV
structure.title: Three invalids, a list and a cheese
structure.summary: J., George and Harris compare symptoms, decide that they are overworked, and settle on a fortnight up the Thames. The planning takes four chapters and holds most of the book’s best-known set pieces: the medical dictionary, the tent in the rain, Uncle Podger and his picture, the sermon on lumber, the Liverpool cheeses and a night of packing that ends with the butter in the teapot.

scenes.title: Three invalids
scenes.summary: The liver-pill circular, a hundred and seven fatal maladies, the doctor’s prescription, the case against a sea trip, and Montmorency outvoted three to one.

scenes.title: Plans discussed
scenes.summary: Camping out on fine nights and on wet ones, a compromise between tent and inn, and a first account of Montmorency, who looks like an angel.

scenes.title: Arrangements settled
scenes.summary: Harris’s method of doing work, Uncle Podger hangs a picture, George’s rule about the things we can’t do without, and the bathing nobody does.

scenes.title: The food question
scenes.summary: Paraffin oil that ruins the sunset, the cheeses from Liverpool, J.’s packing and the tooth-brush, then George and Harris pack the hampers.

structure.label: Chapters V–VIII
structure.title: Waterloo, Kingston and the maze
structure.summary: They oversleep, gather a crowd of errand-boys round the luggage, bribe an engine-driver at Waterloo, and take the boat out from below Kingston bridge. Kingston sets J. musing on Saxon kings, carved oak and china dogs until he steers into the tow-path; Hampton Court reminds Harris of the maze. At Kempton Park they are moved on by a man who wants a shilling, and J. describes Harris singing a comic song.

scenes.title: Mrs. P. arouses us
scenes.summary: The weather forecast, the luggage on the doorstep, Biggs’s boy, and a train that turns out to be the Exeter mail.

scenes.title: Kingston
scenes.summary: Queen Elizabeth’s public-houses, carved oak papered over in blue, the china dog admired in 2288, a collision with the bank, and Harris in the maze.

scenes.title: The river in its Sunday garb
scenes.summary: Boating costume, a picnic with two young women dressed for a photographer’s studio, and Harris’s wish to see Mrs Thomas’s tomb.

scenes.title: Blackmailing
scenes.summary: The man at Kempton Park, the notice-boards of riverside owners, Harris’s comic song, a German song that is not comic, and George buys a banjo.

structure.label: Chapters IX–XII
structure.title: Tow-lines, a first night and Magna Charta
structure.summary: George is put to towing and the tow-line knots itself. After a long haul through Bell Weir lock they camp at Picnic Point, fight the canvas, trick the kettle and eat in silence. Next morning J. imagines King John arriving at the island in 1215, and is then asked to wash up. The pineapple tin that cannot be opened is thrown into the river before Maidenhead, and after they sail into three old anglers George takes the lines up to Marlow.

scenes.title: George is introduced to work
scenes.summary: The heathen instincts of tow-lines, two lovers who lose their boat and tow George’s instead, being towed by girls, and a lock that seems to have vanished.

scenes.title: Our first night
scenes.summary: The hoops and the canvas, the kettle that must not be watched, supper, the tyranny of the stomach, and a restless night under cover.

scenes.title: How George got up early
scenes.summary: A cold bathe, George’s shirt dropped in the river, Harris’s scrambled eggs, and the historical retrospect of June 1215.

scenes.title: Henry VIII. and Anne Boleyn
scenes.summary: Lovers in a house, a night search for rooms at Datchet on an earlier trip, no mustard, the battle with the pineapple tin, Maidenhead, sailing, and three fishers cursing.

structure.label: Chapters XIII–XVI
structure.title: Steam launches, a stew and the woman in the river
structure.summary: Marlow, Bisham and Medmenham supply history to retell; Montmorency squares up to a cat and thinks better of it. The three obstruct every steam launch they meet, make an Irish stew from everything left in the hampers, and remember past disasters with rafts, punts and sails. Above Reading a friend’s launch tows them, and J. finds launches delightful. Near Goring they find a drowned woman, and for a page the book stops joking.

scenes.title: Marlow
scenes.summary: Bisham Abbey, the Medmenham monks, Montmorency and the Tom cat, a procession out of Marlow, and useful methods for annoying steam launches.

scenes.title: Wargrave
scenes.summary: Sonning, the Irish stew and Montmorency’s water-rat, the fight with the kettle, George’s banjo, and Harris and the swans.

scenes.title: Household duties
scenes.summary: Love of work, the old river hand and what he says he has done, early boating memories, punting, and a first experience of sailing.

scenes.title: Reading
scenes.summary: A tow from a steam launch, the irritating behaviour of small boats, the dead woman in the water, and Streatley and Goring.

structure.label: Chapters XVII–XIX
structure.title: A plaster trout, Oxford and a toast in London
structure.summary: Two days at Streatley to get the washing done, and a digression on anglers that ends with the plaster trout. They pull past Wallingford, Dorchester and Abingdon to Oxford, where Montmorency finds dogs enough to fight. The rain begins on the way back down. At Pangbourne they leave the boat with the boatman on a pretext, take the train to Paddington, go to the Alhambra, and drink to being out of it.

scenes.title: Washing day
scenes.summary: Clothes ruined by George’s method, the art of angling, a conscientious fly-fisher, and the trout in the inn parlour.

scenes.title: Locks
scenes.summary: The photograph at Hampton Court lock, Wallingford, Dorchester and Abingdon, and the difficult water between Iffley and Oxford.

scenes.title: Oxford
scenes.summary: The hired up-river boat, the river in the rain, George’s banjo, the flight from Pangbourne and supper after the ballet.

characters.name: J.
characters.role: The narrator; a writer who believes he is industrious, practical and robust
characters.summary: He is never named beyond the initial the others use. He finds he has every disease in the dictionary but one, packs better than any man living, loves work so much he cannot bear to part with it, and hates steam launches until one tows him. Nearly every joke in the book passes through his account of himself, and the account is always a little more flattering than the events it reports. He also writes the purple passages, and is the one who breaks them off.
characters.clue: He sits on the finished Gladstone bag to strap it, and is then asked whether he has put the boots in.

relationships.label: shares the boat and the blame with

characters.name: George
characters.role: A bank clerk, the sleepiest of the three and the one with the sensible ideas
characters.summary: He goes to sleep at a bank from ten to four, as J. puts it, and has to be fetched from the City. He proposes the river, lays down the rule about things you cannot do without, reads out the weather forecast, learns the banjo, and is behind several of the disasters, from flannels washed in the Thames to the trout-case he pulls off the wall. Jerome drew him from his friend George Wingrave.
characters.clue: He asks what time he should wake the others, and is found asleep before anybody answers.

relationships.label: disputes who has done the work with

characters.name: William Samuel Harris
characters.role: The practical one, who always knows a place round the corner
characters.summary: Harris is appetite and certainty. He is sure of the maze, sure he can sing a comic song, sure of his scrambled eggs, and sure that the answer to any mood is a drink. J. makes him the book’s philistine, with no poetry in him and no yearning for the unattainable, and then gives him the last word. Jerome drew him partly from Carl Hentschel, a teetotaller, so the drinking is a joke about a type rather than a portrait.
characters.clue: He leads twenty people into the Hampton Court maze to show them the way out, and they are rescued by an old keeper back from his dinner.

relationships.label: trades insults and shirks work with
will grow up into, says J.,

characters.name: Montmorency
characters.role: A fox terrier, and the fourth member of the party
characters.summary: He looks like an angel sent to earth in the shape of a small dog and behaves like a street fighter: a dozen chickens, a hundred and fourteen fights, rats killed against time. He is the only member of the party who states his view of the trip plainly, that there is nothing in it for him, and he is not far wrong. On the river he attacks a kettle, spares a cat, and brings a dead water-rat to the stew. His idea of heaven turns out to be Oxford, which is full of dogs.
characters.clue: He fights the kettle, loses, and thereafter sits on the bank whenever tea is made.

relationships.label: is landed with a frying-pan by

characters.name: Uncle Podger
characters.role: J.’s uncle, the family man who puts up a picture
characters.summary: He exists for one set piece in chapter III, told to show what Harris will become. Offered a picture to hang, he mobilises the whole house, sends out for nails, loses the coat he is sitting on, measures, loses the mark, falls on the piano, smashes his thumb, and at midnight admires a crooked picture on a ruined wall. Aunt Maria’s response is to ask for notice next time, so that she can spend the week with her mother.
characters.clue: He tells the family to leave everything to him, and then needs half the household round the chair.

characters.name: J.’s doctor
characters.role: His medical man and old chum
characters.summary: He usually feels J.’s pulse and talks about the weather for nothing. Presented with a patient who claims every disease except housemaid’s knee, he thumps him on the chest, butts him with his head and writes a prescription no chemist can make up: beefsteak, beer, a ten-mile walk, bed at eleven, and no more reading. He is the book’s first straight man, and the cure he orders is more or less the holiday the three go on to take and fail at.
characters.clue: His prescription is handed back by the chemist, who explains that he is only a chemist.

characters.name: Biggs’s boy
characters.role: The greengrocer’s errand-boy, who gathers the crowd on the doorstep
characters.summary: Biggs the greengrocer is said to employ the most abandoned errand-boys civilisation has yet produced, and his latest leans on the railings, chews a straw and settles in to watch the luggage. Within minutes the grocer’s boy, the boot-shop boy and the pot-boy from the Blue Posts have joined him, and the street is debating whether it is a wedding or a funeral. He sees the party off with a carrot.
characters.clue: He tells the crowd that the three men are off to find Stanley.

characters.name: The engine-driver at Waterloo
characters.role: Driver of an unidentified train on the high-level platform
characters.summary: Nobody at Waterloo knows where the 11.5 for Kingston goes from, and this man cannot say for certain what train he is driving either. For half a crown he agrees to be the Kingston train, on the reasonable grounds that some train has to go there. The three men learn afterwards that they travelled on the Exeter mail. He is the book’s portrait of Victorian organisation, and he is entirely obliging.
characters.clue: He thinks he may be the 9.32 for Virginia Water or the 10 a.m. express for the Isle of Wight.

characters.name: The drowned woman
characters.role: Unnamed; found in the river near Goring
characters.summary: She is the one death in the book, and J. tells her story as a tract: a woman who had sinned, shut out by respectable relations, keeping herself and a child on twelve shillings a week, who kisses the child, buys it a penny box of chocolate and takes a ticket to Goring. The comedy stops for her, though not entirely, and the passage shows what the book leaves out the rest of the time: people who cannot afford a fortnight on the river.
characters.clue: George lays hold of something black floating on the water, and draws back with a blanched face.

relationships.label: the river’s other story, set beside the holiday of

themes.name: Work, idleness and who is doing it
themes.summary: The holiday begins with a diagnosis of overwork made by three men whose chief symptom is a disinclination to work of any kind. From there the book never stops counting labour: who packs, who tows, who sculls, who steers, who washes up. Each man is sure he is doing everything. The joke is old, but Jerome gives it to a new class of reader, the clerk with a fixed holiday, for whom rest is something earned and rowing is work pretending to be pleasure.
themes.development: A disease called laziness in chapter I, Harris’s method of doing work in III, J. superintending the packing in IV, George introduced to the tow-line in IX, the confession of love for work in XV, and a boat abandoned in XIX.

themes.name: The flattering self-portrait
themes.summary: J. is never caught in a lie. He reports what happened and what he thought of himself, and the two do not match. He packs better than any man living and forgets the boots; he hates steam launches until he is towed by one; he is careful of his work and never touches it. Harris and George get the same treatment through his eyes, which lets the reader enjoy the others’ vanity and miss the narrator’s until it is pointed out.
themes.development: Every disease but one; the expert packer; Harris in the maze and at the piano; the posers at the lock; the trout that four men caught; and the pretence, in the rain, that Nature is beautiful even in her tears.

themes.name: The war with things
themes.summary: Objects in the book have wills, and they are hostile. Tow-lines knit themselves into antimacassars, kettles refuse to boil while watched, canvas hoops nip and attack, a tin of pineapple defeats three men and a mast, and a tooth-brush haunts its owner. The comedy lets the men blame the world for their own incompetence, and it describes something real about a holiday that needs more equipment than the life it was meant to escape.
themes.development: The luggage heap and the packing in IV, the tow-line in IX, the hoops and kettle in X, the pineapple tin in XII, the potatoes in XIV and the plaster trout in XVII.

themes.name: Friendship as a running quarrel
themes.summary: The three are old friends and speak to one another almost entirely in insults, complaints and accusations of shirking. Nobody in the book says he is fond of anyone. The friendship shows itself in other ways: a shared sense of grievance, jokes at each other’s expense, and the moment in the rain when each sees his own mean thoughts in the others’ faces and they run for the train together.
themes.development: The motion carried three to one, the tent that each man thinks the other is spoiling, the wet shirt, the swans, and a toast drunk together after deserting the boat.

themes.name: Nature, sentiment and the weather
themes.summary: The river gets the book’s most ambitious prose: sunsets personified, the moon kissing the water, woods in their spring dress. Jerome writes these passages with conviction and then lets somebody ask about rain. The weather is the other half of the argument. Forecasts are always wrong, the barometer points to set fair in a flood, and in the last chapter the golden fairy stream turns into a spirit-haunted water through the land of vain regrets.
themes.development: The purple passage and Harris’s question in II, the lumber sermon in III, the weather forecast in V, Cliveden woods in XII, and the rain on the way down in XIX.

themes.name: History on the riverbank
themes.summary: Every town the boat passes has a past, and J. retells it: Saxon kings at Kingston, Queen Elizabeth in every public-house, King John at Runnymede, Henry VIII courting at Ankerwyke, Parliament fleeing plague to Reading. Some of it is pageant, written straight; much of it is deflated by a detail from the present. The book also knows that the past is partly a trick of distance, as in J.’s prediction that his landlady’s china dog will one day be a treasure.
themes.development: Kyningestun and the china dog in VI, the pageant of 1215 in XI, the wet shirt that ends it in XII, Bisham and Medmenham in XIII, and Reading’s history in XVI.

themes.name: Clerks, swells and a crowded river
themes.summary: The Thames in 1889 was a pleasure-ground contested by different kinds of money. Riverside owners put up chains and notice-boards, steam launches whistle rowing boats out of the way, Maidenhead is full of swells and showy hotels, and the three men, who describe themselves as without position or influence, resent all of it. The book is written from the rowing boat and for its readers. Its narrator is also quite ready to look down on errand-boys, riverside roughs and anybody with less than he has.
themes.development: Biggs’s boy and the Waterloo porters in V, the Kempton Park blackmailer and the notice-boards in VIII, Maidenhead in XII, the launches in XIII and XVI, and the woman on twelve shillings a week in XVI.

techniques.name: Bathos
techniques.definition: A drop from the elevated to the trivial, usually at the end of a sentence or passage.
techniques.inThisBook: The book’s signature. A page of moonlight ends with Harris asking about rain; a sermon on the boat of life breaks off with I beg your pardon; the barons at Runnymede give way to a frying-pan polished with George’s wet shirt. Jerome has to write the fine passage well enough to carry the reader some distance, or the fall would not be felt.

techniques.name: The comic list
techniques.definition: A list whose items escalate, clash or run on past the point of sense.
techniques.inThisBook: The chapter arguments are lists; so are the diseases in the British Museum, the luggage on the doorstep, the Waterloo platforms, the helpers round Uncle Podger’s chair and the geometric shapes of the pineapple tin. The last item usually carries the joke.

techniques.name: Digression and anecdote
techniques.definition: A departure from the main narrative into a story, reflection or piece of information suggested by the moment.
techniques.inThisBook: The journey is a thread on which anecdotes hang: Uncle Podger, the cheeses, Harris in the maze, the comic song, the trout. The book’s own chapter arguments list them like items on a programme, and the narrator often forgets he is steering while he tells them.

techniques.name: Mock-heroic
techniques.definition: Treating a trivial matter in the language and form of epic, war or tragedy.
techniques.inThisBook: The pineapple tin is a battle with a relic kept afterwards; the tent is a life-and-death struggle; notice-boards and steam launches provoke fantasies of murder and burial; the paraffin oil is renounced by an awful oath under a blasted oak.

techniques.name: Personification
techniques.definition: Giving human motives, feelings or speech to animals and objects.
techniques.inThisBook: Montmorency speaks his objections outright, and the equipment has characters too: the tow-line with its unrespectable habits, the kettle that sulks when watched, the hoops that attack from behind, and the tin that grins.

techniques.name: Deadpan
techniques.definition: Reporting absurd events in a level, reasonable voice that never admits they are absurd.
techniques.inThisBook: J. describes a horse terrified into four miles an hour by cheese, a train that agrees to be another train, and a man who has had every disease since boyhood, all in the tone of a sensible witness. Understatement is its common form: Harris, in the middle of a mob, feels he has to a certain extent become unpopular.

techniques.name: The unreliable narrator
techniques.definition: A narrator whose account the reader learns to read against, because he misjudges himself or what he reports.
techniques.inThisBook: J. is honest about events and wrong about himself. He claims energy, expertise and fairness in the same sentences that show idleness, incompetence and self-interest, and the book leaves the reader to set his opinions side by side, as with the steam launches of chapters XIII and XVI.

quotations.text: I plodded conscientiously through the twenty-six letters, and the only malady I could conclude I had not got was housemaid’s knee.
quotations.context: J. has gone to the British Museum to read up on hay fever and has worked through the whole medical dictionary.
quotations.analysis: The joke is built like a proof. J. goes through the alphabet as a conscientious student would, so the absurd conclusion arrives by method, and the one exception becomes the punchline. The next paragraph improves it: he feels slighted not to have housemaid’s knee, then grows less grasping and decides to do without. Hypochondria becomes acquisitiveness, a man collecting diseases. And the missing one is a servant’s complaint, the ailment of kneeling to scrub, which a man who never does that could hardly catch.

quotations.text: 1 ten-mile walk every morning. 1 bed at 11 sharp every night. And don’t stuff up your head with things you don’t understand.
quotations.speaker: J.’s doctor
quotations.context: The end of the prescription, which a chemist has just handed back unmade; it begins with a pound of beefsteak and a pint of bitter beer every six hours.
quotations.analysis: The prescription is funny because of its form. It is set out like a dosage, with quantities and hours, so the chemist reasonably cannot make it up; the medicine is steak, beer, exercise and bed. Then the last line drops the formula and speaks plainly, and it is aimed at the reading-room where J. caught his diseases. The doctor is the book’s first straight man, and he diagnoses the whole party: nothing is wrong that fresh air and fewer books will not cure.

quotations.text: From my earliest infancy I have been a martyr to it. As a boy, the disease hardly ever left me for a day. They did not know, then, that it was my liver. Medical science was in a far less advanced state than now, and they used to put it down to laziness.
quotations.context: The chief symptom in the liver-pill circular is a general disinclination to work of any kind.
quotations.analysis: The deadpan keeps the vocabulary of medicine while the facts describe idleness. Martyr, disease, medical science are solemn words; the symptom is not wanting to work, and the old treatment was a clump on the head, which J. admits often worked. The reader supplies the diagnosis the narrator refuses to make. It is also the book’s first statement of its real subject: three young men who call their boredom overwork and prescribe themselves a holiday.

quotations.text: There’s nothing for me to do. Scenery is not in my line, and I don’t smoke. If I see a rat, you won’t stop; and if I go to sleep, you get fooling about with the boat, and slop me overboard. If you ask me, I call the whole thing bally foolishness.
quotations.speaker: Montmorency
quotations.context: George has proposed the river and the other two have agreed; the dog lodges an objection.
quotations.analysis: Montmorency is the only member of the party allowed to speak without irony, and his objections are exact: a rowing holiday offers a dog no rats, no smoking and no scenery he cares for. The comedy is in the register. J. gives him the grumble of a man dragged on somebody else’s holiday, and through him the book says what none of the men will admit about their plan. The motion is then carried three to one, like a committee vote, and the minority report is the accurate one.

quotations.text: we fall asleep beneath the great, still stars, and dream that the world is young again … Harris said: “How about when it rained?”
quotations.context: J. and George favour camping out, and J. describes a night by the river in a single long, lyrical sentence.
quotations.analysis: The sentence runs for most of a page, through the moon’s sister’s kiss and the wiles of painted civilisation, and Harris answers it in five words. The fall works only because J. writes the passage in earnest enough to carry the reader a little way. It also sets out the friendship: J. supplies the feeling and Harris the practical question, and the book gives Harris the better of it, since the next two pages describe exactly what happens to a tent in the rain.

quotations.text: That’s Harris all over—so ready to take the burden of everything himself, and put it on the backs of other people.
quotations.context: Harris has offered to make the list, provided J. gets the paper, George the grocery catalogue, and somebody the pencil.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a trap that closes in its last clause. It opens as praise, ready to take the burden of everything himself, and the final phrase reverses it without any change of tone. That shape, a generous start and a treacherous finish, is one of Jerome’s commonest devices. It also doubles back on the speaker. A page later J. rescues Harris from overwork by giving the paper, the pencil and the catalogue to the others and announcing that he will do the work.

quotations.text: “There you are,” he would say, stepping heavily off the chair on to the charwoman’s corns, and surveying the mess he had made with evident pride. “Why, some people would have had a man in to do a little thing like that!”
quotations.speaker: Uncle Podger
quotations.context: Midnight. The picture is up, crooked, and the wall for yards round looks as if it has been smoothed with a rake.
quotations.analysis: The boast is funny because the reader has watched the evening: seven helpers, a lost coat, a cut finger, a smashed thumb, a hammer through the plaster. The charwoman’s corns and the evident pride share a sentence, the cost and the satisfaction side by side. Would say marks the habit; this is a man who does it every time. The digression is told as a portrait of Harris but works as a model of the whole trip: a small job, a household mobilised, and a man sure of his own competence standing on somebody’s foot.

quotations.text: You will have time to think as well as to work. Time to drink in life’s sunshine—time to listen to the Æolian music that the wind of God draws from the human heart-strings around us—time to— I beg your pardon, really. I quite forgot.
quotations.context: George’s rule for packing, only what we can’t do without, has grown into a sermon about throwing life’s lumber overboard.
quotations.analysis: A sensible remark about hampers becomes a sermon, the sermon a list of the lumber people carry through life, and the list a lyrical catalogue of sunbeams and forget-me-nots. Then the voice breaks off mid-phrase and apologises. The bathos is aimed at J.: he has been caught preaching, and I quite forgot implies he does it often. The sermon is not simply mocked, though. Its advice, a light boat, one or two friends, someone to love, is the book’s sincerest statement, and Jerome lets it stand before he laughs at the man making it.

quotations.text: My friend got rid of them, at last, by taking them down to a sea-side town, and burying them on the beach. It gained the place quite a reputation. Visitors said they had never noticed before how strong the air was, and weak-chested and consumptive people used to throng there for years afterwards.
quotations.context: The end of the story of the Liverpool cheeses, told to support George’s rule that no cheese goes in the hamper.
quotations.analysis: The cheese story is a digression inside a digression, and each stage is the same joke at a larger scale: the smell wakes a somnambulist cab-horse into a gallop of four miles an hour, empties a railway carriage, drives a wife and children to a hotel, sickens the bargemen and outrages a coroner. The ending turns the escalation into advertising. A resort’s bracing air is a buried cheese, and the invalids who flock there are the book’s hypochondriacs seen from outside. Deadpan keeps it all plausible: nobody in the story ever admits the absurdity.

quotations.text: Anyhow, if he wasn’t the 11.5 for Kingston, he said he was pretty confident he was the 9.32 for Virginia Water, or the 10 a.m. express for the Isle of Wight, or somewhere in that direction, and we should all know when we got there. We slipped half-a-crown into his hand, and begged him to be the 11.5 for Kingston.
quotations.context: At Waterloo, after porters, the station-master and the traffic superintendent have each named a different platform.
quotations.analysis: Nobody at Waterloo knows where any train goes, and Jerome escalates the ignorance in lists: platform two, platform one, the local, the Southampton express, the Windsor loop, and now the driver’s own three candidates. The solution is not information but a bribe, and begged him to be the 11.5 treats a train as something a man can choose to become. The joke is about the new machinery of Victorian leisure, timetables and officials, and how little it resembles the order it promises. The train turns out to be the Exeter mail.

quotations.text: In 2288 people will gush over it. The making of such dogs will have become a lost art. Our descendants will wonder how we did it, and say how clever we were. We shall be referred to lovingly as “those grand old artists that flourished in the nineteenth century, and produced those china dogs.”
quotations.context: Carved oak in a Kingston shop, papered over in blue to make the room cheerful, has set J. thinking about what makes an antique.
quotations.analysis: The musing ends in the future. J. has described his landlady’s china dog without mercy, its expression amiability carried to verge of imbecility, and now imagines it dug up legless and admired in a glass case. The comedy is a transfer of value by time: he mocks the collectors of his own day by imagining their descendants, and the prophecy has partly come true, since Victorian pottery dogs are collected now. History in the book is often like this, less a record of greatness than a trick of distance.

quotations.text: Harris drew out his map again, after a while, but the sight of it only infuriated the mob, and they told him to go and curl his hair with it. Harris said that he couldn’t help feeling that, to a certain extent, he had become unpopular.
quotations.context: Harris’s story of taking a country cousin into the Hampton Court maze, which he had studied on a map and thought too simple to be worth the twopence.
quotations.analysis: Understatement is the joke. The scene has built a crowd of twenty lost people, a woman with a baby who calls Harris an impostor, and return after return to the centre; to a certain extent, he had become unpopular is the mildest possible summary. The phrasing is Harris’s own, reported by J., so it is also a portrait: Harris survives humiliation by describing it in the language of a committee. The maze is a small model of the river trip, a simple route, a confident guide and a map that makes things worse.

quotations.text: And Harris never sees what an ass he is making of himself, and how he is annoying a lot of people who never did him any harm. He honestly imagines that he has given them a treat, and says he will sing another comic song after supper.
quotations.context: J. has just set out Harris’s performance at a party as a little play, with stage directions for the nervous pianist.
quotations.analysis: The performance itself turns on a muddle. Harris announces the Judge’s song from Trial by Jury, starts the First Lord’s from HMS Pinafore, and fuses the two, so that called to the Bar collides with office-boy to an attorney. The audience roars, and he takes the laughter as a compliment. This sentence adds the moral: Harris does not know, and everyone else does. That gap between a man’s view of his performance and the room’s is the comic engine of the whole book, and J. applies it to everyone except himself.

quotations.text: There may be tow-lines that are a credit to their profession—conscientious, respectable tow-lines—tow-lines that do not imagine they are crochet-work, and try to knit themselves up into antimacassars the instant they are left to themselves.
quotations.context: George has been handed the tow-line, which J. coiled with great care, and it has turned into a tangle in his hands.
quotations.analysis: Jerome gives the rope a moral character. It is not merely tangled; it imagines itself crochet-work, and the hope that some tow-lines may be conscientious and respectable is phrased like a character reference for a servant. Personification lets the men blame the rope for their own clumsiness, which is the book’s steady view of equipment: every object has a will, and it is against them. The domestic comparison matters too. The river is meant to be an escape from the drawing-room, and the rope turns into drawing-room needlework.

quotations.text: That is the only way to get a kettle to boil up the river. If it sees that you are waiting for it and are anxious, it will never even sing.
quotations.context: The first night at Picnic Point. The canvas is at last up, and the kettle has been put on in the nose of the boat and ignored.
quotations.analysis: The proverb says a watched pot never boils. Jerome takes it literally and builds a method on it: the kettle can see and overhear, so the men must turn their backs and shout that they would rather have lemonade, at which it boils over in pique. The joke is the seriousness of the instructions, written like a manual. Like the tow-line, the kettle is a character with a temper, and later Montmorency attacks one by the spout and loses.

quotations.text: A bolder hand might have turned the game even at that point. Had it been a Richard there! the cup of liberty might have been dashed from England’s lips, and the taste of freedom held back for a hundred years.
quotations.context: J.’s imagined June morning of 1215, with King John arriving to be rowed across to the island where the Charter waits.
quotations.analysis: For two pages the comedy stops. J. fills Staines with soldiers and the river with barges, in a present-tense pageant of casques and banners, and writes it straight, excited exclamation and all. The history is the popular kind, a nation’s liberty turning on one king’s nerve. Its placing is the joke. The chapter closes on the cornerstone of England’s temple of liberty, and the next one opens with George asking whether J. would mind helping to wash up.

quotations.text: I was sitting on the bank, conjuring up this scene to myself, when George remarked that when I was quite rested, perhaps I would not mind helping to wash up; and, thus recalled from the days of the glorious past to the prosaic present, with all its misery and sin, I slid down into the boat and cleaned out the frying-pan with a stick of wood and a tuft of grass, polishing it up finally with George’s wet shirt.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the chapter, straight after the pageant of Magna Charta.
quotations.analysis: This is the fall the pageant was built for. The glorious past and the prosaic present, with all its misery and sin, are mock-solemn phrases, and the sentence then descends through a stick of wood and a tuft of grass to its last words. The shirt is a callback: J. dropped it in the river that morning, was furious at George’s laughter until he saw whose shirt it was, and then laughed so much he dropped it again. The bathos works because Jerome let the reader believe in the barons for a while, and because George, the man who interrupted, supplies the dishcloth.

quotations.text: We beat it out flat; we beat it back square; we battered it into every form known to geometry—but we could not make a hole in it.
quotations.context: There is no tin-opener, and a tin of pineapple has already defeated a pocket-knife, a pair of scissors, a hitcher and a mast.
quotations.analysis: The episode is written as a battle, with wounds, a weapon and a survivor who keeps his crushed straw hat as a relic. This sentence is its climax, and the list does the work: flat, square, every form known to geometry, then the plain clause that nothing has changed. Afterwards the tin acquires a dent like a mocking grin and is flung into the river with curses, like a defeated enemy. Three men and a missing tin-opener become a war of the world against its users, and the users lose.

quotations.text: I do hate steam launches: I suppose every rowing man does. I never see a steam launch but I feel I should like to lure it to a lonely part of the river, and there, in the silence and the solitude, strangle it.
quotations.context: Leaving Marlow just before Henley week, when launches are going upstream in numbers, some towing houseboats.
quotations.analysis: J. speaks for every rowing man and wishes on a machine the death of a villain in a melodrama, lured, isolated and strangled. The violence is a joke of proportion, like the tombstone he would make from a notice-board in chapter VIII, but the grievance behind it is real: launches belonged to people with money, and they whistled rowing boats out of the way. The chapter then describes the three drifting across the channel with their backs turned. Three chapters later J. is towed by a launch, and his opinions turn inside out.

quotations.text: It is not that I object to the work, mind you; I like work: it fascinates me. I can sit and look at it for hours. I love to keep it by me: the idea of getting rid of it nearly breaks my heart.
quotations.context: Harris has proposed that George and J. should scull while he steers, and J. feels he is doing more than his share.
quotations.analysis: The paradox works because fascinates is the right word used wrongly. Work becomes first a spectacle, something to watch for hours, and then a possession, kept, dusted and never touched. Every clause sounds like an industrious man’s boast and describes an idle one. J. never concedes the point. He goes on to observe that every man in a boat believes he is doing everything, and does not apply the rule to himself, which is the book’s method with its narrator in one paragraph.

quotations.text: It is very delightful being towed up by a launch. I prefer it myself to rowing. The run would have been more delightful still, if it had not been for a lot of wretched small boats that were continually getting in the way of our launch.
quotations.context: At Reading lock a steam launch belonging to friends of J. takes them in tow almost as far as Streatley.
quotations.analysis: The chapter argument calls this the irritating behaviour of small boats, and the joke is that J. now speaks as he said launch-owners speak. In chapter XIII small boats were a noble resistance; now they are wretched and ought to be run down now and then to teach them a lesson. Jerome never points out the reversal. He leaves the reader to remember, which is how the book treats its narrator throughout: not exposing him, only placing his opinions where they can be compared.

quotations.text: Six shillings a week does not keep body and soul together very unitedly. They want to get away from each other when there is only such a very slight bond as that between them.
quotations.context: The story of the drowned woman they have found in the river, as J. learned it afterwards.
quotations.analysis: The book’s one real death is told as a sentimental tract, a fallen woman shut out by respectable relations, and yet the comic habit of phrasing survives in it. Not keeping body and soul together very unitedly is a turn on a cliché, the same move Jerome makes about cheese and kettles. Here it lands as bitterness: twelve hours a day for twelve shillings, half of it for the child. The passage shows what the comic voice is made of, and it sits between a launch towing three men on holiday and a recommendation of Streatley for a few days’ stay.

quotations.text: And so it would have been strange and unaccountable, if it had been a stuffed trout, but it was not. That trout was plaster-of-Paris.
quotations.context: George has climbed on a chair to look at the trout in the inn parlour and brought the case down.
quotations.analysis: The fish story is a comic form with a fixed shape, in which every angler’s fish grows. Jerome runs it four times in the inn parlour, the weight rising from eighteen pounds to thirty-four, before the landlord tells the real history. Then George falls on the case, the trout breaks into a thousand fragments, or nine hundred, and the last line reverses everything: the object at the centre of five confident stories was never a fish. The joke catches the reader too, who had been sorting the true account from the false.

quotations.text: Our feet were undoubtedly the leading article in that photograph. Indeed, very little else was to be seen.
quotations.context: A memory of a crowded lock at Hampton Court, where a photographer was taking a picture of all the boats.
quotations.analysis: The photograph is a story about posing. George hides his feet and arranges his expression; J. leans on the hitcher with a curl over his forehead and a touch of cynicism, which I am told suits me. Then the boat’s nose catches under the lock timbers, and the camera records them on their backs with their feet in the air. Leading article is newspaper language for the main story, applied to four boots. Vanity and its exposure end up on a single plate, and nobody else will buy a copy.

quotations.text: We pretended, at first, that we enjoyed it. We said it was a change, and that we liked to see the river under all its different aspects. We said we could not expect to have it all sunshine, nor should we wish it. We told each other that Nature was beautiful, even in her tears.
quotations.context: The first day of rowing back down from Oxford in the rain.
quotations.analysis: In the rain the three try to keep up the tone of the book’s own lyrical passages and cannot. Each we said is a line from the sentimental guide to nature, variety, not all sunshine, beautiful even in her tears, and the repetition sounds like people agreeing in order to keep their spirits up. The purple passages of the earlier chapters are here turned into dialogue and exposed as things one says. The chapter has just offered its own fine writing about the river in rain, and this puts it in brackets.

quotations.text: “Well,” said Harris, reaching his hand out for his glass, “we have had a pleasant trip, and my hearty thanks for it to old Father Thames—but I think we did well to chuck it when we did. Here’s to Three Men well out of a Boat!”
quotations.speaker: Harris
quotations.context: Supper in a London restaurant after the Alhambra, with the rain splashing in the street outside.
quotations.analysis: The book ends with the holiday abandoned and its own title turned round. Harris thanks Father Thames in a toastmaster’s phrase and then undoes the whole project in a slang verb, chuck. It is the last bathos and the most honest, since the trip has consisted largely of things going wrong and the best evening in it is spent in town. Montmorency, who voted against the river in chapter I, stands at the window and barks his agreement, so the minority report is carried at last.

timeline.label: Magna Carta is agreed at Runnymede
timeline.detail: In June, on the meadows between Staines and Windsor. Jerome has King John rowed to the island opposite and sign it there, and declines to say which side of the water is right.

timeline.label: Jerome Klapka Jerome is born in Walsall
timeline.detail: On 2 May. He grew up in poverty in east London, and worked as a railway clerk, actor, schoolmaster and journalist before he made a living from books.

timeline.label: HMS Pinafore opens in London
timeline.detail: Gilbert and Sullivan’s comic opera, whose First Lord’s song Harris muddles with the Judge’s song from Trial by Jury in chapter VIII. The First Lord was created by George Grossmith, co-author of The Diary of a Nobody.

timeline.label: Parliament passes the Thames Preservation Act
timeline.detail: Meant to keep the river open for pleasure boating as riverside owners tried to fence off banks and backwaters, the grievance behind J.’s rage at notice-boards and chains.

timeline.label: Jerome's Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow published
timeline.detail: Jerome’s book of comic essays, named on the title page of Three Men in a Boat as his earlier work. Its manner, reflective and self-mocking, is the narrator’s voice here.

timeline.label: Jerome marries Georgina Marris
timeline.detail: In June. The couple spent their honeymoon on the Thames, and the serial began that autumn.

timeline.label: The serial begins in Home Chimes
timeline.detail: Running from September 1888 to June 1889, according to the Jerome K. Jerome Society’s bibliography, before the book appeared.

timeline.label: J. W. Arrowsmith publishes the book in Bristol
timeline.detail: In August, with illustrations by A. Frederics and a preface praising its hopeless and incurable veracity. The same firm published The Diary of a Nobody three years later.

timeline.label: Three Men on the Bummel, the sequel, published
timeline.detail: The sequel sends J., George and Harris on a bicycling tour of Germany.

timeline.label: Arrowsmith advertises 202,000 copies in twenty years
timeline.detail: A publisher’s figure for copies produced, not an audited sales total, and it could not include the unauthorised American editions.

timeline.label: Jerome publishes My Life and Times
timeline.detail: The memoir in which he recalls the book’s origins and its hostile reviews. Some of the reviews he quotes have not been traced to their original issues, so his account is best read as recollection.

timeline.label: Jerome dies at Northampton
timeline.detail: On 14 June, after a stroke suffered on a motoring tour.

timeline.label: Ken Annakin’s film
timeline.detail: A British colour film with David Tomlinson, Jimmy Edwards and Laurence Harvey as the three men.

timeline.label: BBC television adaptation by Tom Stoppard
timeline.detail: Directed by Stephen Frears, with Michael Palin, Tim Curry and Stephen Moore in the boat.

places.name: Kingston upon Thames
places.note: The boat waits just below the bridge; Harris takes the sculls and J. the tiller-lines. They reach it from Waterloo on a train that turns out to be the Exeter mail.

places.name: Hampton Court Palace
places.note: The old river wall J. wants to paint, the maze where Harris gets twenty people lost, and the lock where George and J. are photographed feet first.

places.name: Runnymede and Magna Charta Island
places.note: The party’s first camp is at Picnic Point near the island, and next morning J. imagines King John being rowed across to it in 1215.

places.name: Marlow
places.note: Where they leave the boat by the bridge and put up for the night, and where, on an earlier trip, not even a walk out of town could escape the paraffin oil.

places.name: Streatley and Goring
places.note: The drowned woman had come down by train to Goring. The three stay two days at Streatley to get their washing done, and meet the plaster trout on the way back from a walk to Wallingford.

places.name: Oxford, Folly Bridge
places.note: The top of the journey, reached after the difficult water below Iffley; Montmorency’s idea of heaven, because it is full of dogs to fight.

places.name: Pangbourne
places.note: Where the three men leave the boat at the Swan in the rain, tell the boatman they will be back at nine, and creep off to the railway station.

places.name: The Alhambra, Leicester Square
places.note: The music hall where the deserters, in dirty flannels and battered hats, are mistaken for a troupe of contortionists, before supper and the final toast.

criticalViews.position: The comic book of the clerk class
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the book belongs to its readers: clerks, bank employees and shop assistants with a fixed fortnight’s holiday, reading cheap weeklies, speaking a slangy suburban English. Jerome gives them a holiday in their own idiom, and its popularity with that audience and the distaste of some reviewers are two sides of the same fact. Jerome’s own later memory was that the press attacked its vulgarity.
criticalViews.counter: The idiom is new but the machinery is old: the mock-heroic battle, the sermon, the historical pageant, the sentimental set piece. And the narrator is not the champion of the lower-middle class he is sometimes taken for. He sneers at errand-boys and riverside roughs as readily as at swells, and his memory of a hostile press is itself partly unverified.

criticalViews.position: The purple passages are there to be punctured
criticalViews.summary: The lyrical and historical interludes are parodies of guidebook prose and sentimental nature writing. Every sunset ends in a question about rain, every pageant in washing up, and the reader is meant to enjoy the fall more than the flight.
criticalViews.counter: Not all of them fall. Cliveden woods, much of the Runnymede pageant and the drowned woman are left standing, and Jerome said he set out to write a guide to the river. The book runs on two sincerities at once: it means the fine writing, and it means the collapse. Reading it as parody alone misses why the parody works.

criticalViews.position: A holiday from women and home
criticalViews.summary: The trip is an escape into male company from domestic life, and women appear only at its edges: landladies, a wife driven out by cheese, two girls dressed for a photograph, a fallen woman in the river. The comedy depends on that absence.
criticalViews.counter: The book knows what it is escaping and does not flatter the escape. Its best domestic scene, Uncle Podger, is seen from the family’s side and makes the man the fool; the three men are most helpless when doing housework; and the voyage ends back in town with clean napkins and a proper supper.

essayQuestions.question: How does Jerome make comedy out of the gap between what J. says about himself and what he does?
essayQuestions.focus: Narrator, self-deception and the reader’s judgement
plan: Start with the hypochondria of chapter I, where a disinclination to work is diagnosed as a liver complaint and a clump on the head is the cure.
Show the pattern in chapter IV: the expert packer who forgets the boots, and the energetic nature that wants to superintend.
Set the steam launches of chapter XIII beside the tow of chapter XVI, and note that Jerome never points out the reversal.
Analyse I like work: it fascinates me, where each clause sounds like a boast and describes idleness.
Conclude on how the book treats all three men this way, and why J.’s good humour keeps the reader on his side.

essayQuestions.question: Explore the use of bathos in Three Men in a Boat. Is the book mocking its lyrical passages or indulging them?
essayQuestions.focus: Register, sentiment and the purple passage
plan: Analyse the night by the river in chapter II and Harris’s five-word reply.
Look at the lumber sermon in chapter III and how I beg your pardon, really, turns the joke on the preacher.
Follow the Runnymede pageant into the wet shirt that ends it at the start of chapter XII.
Consider passages that are not deflated, such as Cliveden woods and the drowned woman, and what they suggest about Jerome’s intentions.
Weigh the answer: the fall is felt only because the flight was meant.

essayQuestions.question: Why do objects cause so much trouble in Three Men in a Boat?
essayQuestions.focus: Personification, mock-heroic and the equipment of leisure
plan: Set out the equipment problem in chapters III and IV: a list that will not fit in a boat, and packing that ends in chaos.
Analyse the personified tow-line and the kettle that must not be watched.
Read the pineapple tin as mock-heroic battle, with its mocking grin and its burial at sea.
Consider what the war with things lets the men avoid admitting about themselves.
Relate it to the lumber sermon: a book about travelling light that cannot stop accumulating.

essayQuestions.question: What does the book suggest about the friendship between J., George and Harris?
essayQuestions.focus: Friendship, quarrel and the comic group
plan: Note that affection is never stated, and trace the quarrels about work from the tent in chapter II to the rota in chapter XV.
Look at how each man is used as a foil: J.’s sentiment, Harris’s appetite, George’s gloom.
Examine shared jokes against one another, such as the wet shirt, the swans and the photograph.
Analyse the flight from Pangbourne, when each sees his own guilty thoughts in the others’ faces.
End on the toast, and what it means that the friendship is happiest out of the boat.

discussionQuestions: Montmorency is the only character who says exactly what he thinks. Why might Jerome give that job to a dog?
Harris thinks he is giving the room a treat when he sings. Is J. any different when he writes a purple passage?
The drowned woman is the one serious episode in the book. Does it belong, or does it break the book in two?
J. hates steam launches until one tows him. Where else does the book let an opinion change with a man’s circumstances?
Does the book make you want to go up the river, or persuade you not to?
The three men give up and go to a music hall. Is that a failure, or the most honest ending the book could have?

related.why: Published by the same Bristol firm three years later, another comic first person who reports his own failures without seeing them; and Harris’s song was created on stage by one of its authors.
The same river two decades on, messed about in by animals rather than clerks, with the lyrical passages played straight and a motor-car where Jerome had steam launches.
A close reading of Dickens’s singing kettle, the ancestor of Jerome’s kettle that refuses to boil while anyone is watching.
Written the same year on the same Thames, going the other way: a police launch racing downstream past the marshes while Jerome’s boat drifts up to Oxford.
Another comic river journey told by a narrator who understands less than the reader, where the river is freedom and the shore keeps interrupting.
